column1: In economics, what is a market?
column2: Any arrangement where buyers and sellers of goods, services or resources are linked together to carry out an exchange.

column1: Must buyers and sellers meet face to face for a market to exist?
column2: No. A market can be one physical place (e.g. a vegetable market) or many places (e.g. the oil market); buyers and sellers can communicate by phone, internet, ads or any method that conveys information about price, quantity and quality.

column1: Distinguish between local, national and international markets, with an example of each.
column2:
Local: buyers and sellers come from a local area (e.g. a neighbourhood bakery).
National: from anywhere within one country (e.g. most labour markets).
International: from anywhere in the world (e.g. the world oil market).

column1: Distinguish between product markets and resource (factor) markets.
column2:
Product markets: goods and services are bought and sold.
Resource (factor) markets: factors of production are bought and sold.

column1: What does 'competition' mean in its everyday (non-technical) sense?
column2: A process in which rivals compete to achieve some objective, e.g. firms competing over sales, consumers over a scarce product, workers over the best jobs, countries over export markets.

column1: What does 'competition' mean in microeconomics?
column2: A situation with many buyers and sellers acting independently, so that no one has the ability to influence the price at which the product is sold.

column1: What is market power (also called monopoly power)?
column2: The control that a seller has over the price of the product it sells.

column1: How is the degree of competition between sellers related to their market power?
column2: Inversely: the greater the competition between sellers, the smaller their market power and the weaker their control over price; the greater the market power, the greater the control over price.

column1: What is a competitive market?
column2: A market with large numbers of buyers and sellers acting independently, so no individual seller (or small group of sellers) can control price; price is determined by the interaction of demand and supply.

column1: What is the demand of an individual consumer for a good?
column2: The various quantities of the good (or service) the consumer is willing and able to buy at different possible prices during a particular time period, ceteris paribus.

column1: In the definition of demand, what do 'willing' and 'able' mean?
column2: Willing: the consumer wants to buy the good. Able: the consumer can afford it. Both are needed: wanting a Ferrari you cannot afford (or affording one you do not want) is not demand.

column1: In demand analysis, what does ceteris paribus mean?
column2: All things other than price that can affect how much consumers are willing and able to buy (e.g. income, tastes, prices of related goods) are assumed to stay constant.

column1: What is a demand schedule?
column2: A table listing the quantities of a good that a consumer (or the market) is willing and able to buy at various prices.

column1: State the law of demand.
column2: There is a negative relationship between the price of a good and its quantity demanded over a particular time period, ceteris paribus: price ↑ → quantity demanded ↓; price ↓ → quantity demanded ↑.

column1: Why is the relationship described by the law of demand called both 'negative' and 'causal'?
column2: Negative (indirect): price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions. Causal: changes in price cause the changes in quantity demanded.

column1: Describe a demand curve diagram (axes and slope).
column2: Price (P) on the vertical axis, quantity (Q) on the horizontal axis. The demand curve slopes downward from left to right, showing the negative relationship between price and quantity demanded. It is called a 'curve' even when drawn as a straight line.

column1: Does a demand curve tell us how much consumers will actually buy and at what price?
column2: No. It only shows how much consumers would be willing and able to buy at each possible price; the actual price and quantity are determined by the interaction of demand with supply.

column1: What is market demand?
column2: The total quantities of a good that all consumers in a market are willing and able to buy at different prices over a period of time, ceteris paribus: the sum of all individual demands.

column1: How is the market demand curve derived from individual demand curves?
column2: At each possible price, add up the quantities demanded by every individual consumer (horizontal summation). Plotting these totals at every price gives the market demand curve.

column1: Why can two consumers have different demand curves for the same good?
column2: They have different preferences, so they are willing and able to buy different quantities at each price.

column1: What are the non-price determinants of demand?
column2: The variables other than price that influence demand (e.g. income, tastes, prices of related goods, number of consumers). They are the variables held constant by the ceteris paribus assumption.

column1: On a demand diagram, what does a rightward shift of the demand curve show, and what is it called?
column2: More is demanded at every given price. It is called an increase in demand.

column1: On a demand diagram, what does a leftward shift of the demand curve show, and what is it called?
column2: Less is demanded at every given price. It is called a decrease in demand.

column1: What is a normal good?
column2: A good whose demand increases when consumer income increases (demand varies directly with income). Most goods are normal goods.

column1: Consumer income rises. What happens to the demand for a normal good?
column2: Income ↑ → consumers willing and able to buy more at every price → demand ↑ → demand curve shifts right. (Income ↓ → shifts left.)

column1: What is an inferior good? Give an example.
column2: A good whose demand falls when consumer income increases (demand varies inversely with income), e.g. second-hand clothes, used cars, bus tickets.

column1: Consumer income rises. What happens to the demand for an inferior good, and why?
column2: Income ↑ → consumers switch to more expensive alternatives (e.g. new clothes, cars instead of buses) → demand for the inferior good ↓ → demand curve shifts left. (Income ↓ → shifts right.)

column1: How do changes in tastes and preferences shift the demand curve for a product?
column2:
Tastes change in favour of the product (it becomes more popular) → demand ↑ → curve shifts right.
Tastes change against it (e.g. a report that it harms health) → demand ↓ → curve shifts left.

column1: What are substitute goods? Give an example.
column2: Two goods that satisfy a similar need, so one can be used in place of the other, e.g. Coca-Cola and Pepsi, apples and oranges, milk and yoghurt.

column1: The price of Coca-Cola falls. What happens to the demand for Pepsi?
column2: They are substitutes: price of Coca-Cola ↓ → some consumers switch from Pepsi to Coca-Cola → demand for Pepsi ↓ → Pepsi's demand curve shifts left.

column1: For substitute goods X and Y, in which direction do the price of X and the demand for Y move?
column2: In the same direction: price of X ↑ → demand for Y ↑ (shifts right); price of X ↓ → demand for Y ↓ (shifts left).

column1: What are complementary goods? Give an example.
column2: Goods that tend to be used together, e.g. computers and software, shoes and shoelaces, tennis balls and tennis rackets.

column1: The price of computers falls. What happens to the demand for computer software?
column2: They are complements: price of computers ↓ → more computers bought → demand for software ↑ → software's demand curve shifts right.

column1: For complementary goods X and Y, in which direction do the price of X and the demand for Y move?
column2: In opposite directions: price of X ↓ → demand for Y ↑ (shifts right); price of X ↑ → demand for Y ↓ (shifts left).

column1: What are independent goods? Give an example.
column2: Goods that are unrelated, so a change in the price of one has little or no effect on demand for the other (e.g. pencils and apples, cars and ice cream). Most goods are independent of each other.

column1: How does a change in the number of consumers affect market demand?
column2: Number of consumers ↑ → market demand ↑ → demand curve shifts right (and vice versa), because market demand is the sum of all individual demands.

column1: Distinguish between a 'change in quantity demanded' and a 'change in demand'.
column2:
Change in quantity demanded: caused by a change in the good's own price; shown as a movement along the demand curve.
Change in demand: caused by a change in a non-price determinant; shown as a shift of the whole demand curve.

column1: A good's price falls, ceteris paribus. Describe what happens on its demand diagram and name the change.
column2: A movement down along the same demand curve (e.g. point A to point B) to a larger quantity. This is an increase in quantity demanded; the curve does not shift.

column1: A good's price rises, ceteris paribus. Describe what happens on its demand diagram and name the change.
column2: A movement up along the same demand curve (e.g. point B to point A) to a smaller quantity. This is a decrease in quantity demanded; the curve does not shift.

column1: The number of buyers of a good falls. Describe what happens on its demand diagram and name the change.
column2: The entire demand curve shifts left (e.g. D1 to D3): less is demanded at every price. This is a decrease in demand.

column1: Why does a change in a good's own price not shift its demand curve?
column2: The demand curve already shows how quantity demanded responds to every possible price, so a price change is a movement along it. Only changes in non-price determinants (held constant under ceteris paribus) shift the curve.

column1: What is utility?
column2: The satisfaction consumers gain from consuming something. It is subjective, since it depends on personal tastes and preferences.

column1: How is utility measured in the theory of consumer behaviour?
column2: It cannot really be measured, but for building the theory it is assumed to be quantifiable in imaginary units called utils.

column1: Distinguish between total utility and marginal utility.
column2:
Total utility: the total satisfaction from consuming a good.
Marginal utility: the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit of it.

column1: State the law of diminishing marginal utility.
column2: As consumption of a good increases, the marginal utility (extra satisfaction) from each additional unit consumed decreases.

column1: As a consumer buys more units of a good, what happens to total utility while marginal utility is falling but positive, at zero, and negative?
column2:
Positive but falling MU: total utility still rises, but by less each time.
MU of zero: total utility is at its maximum.
Negative MU: total utility falls.

column1: How does the law of diminishing marginal utility explain the law of demand?
column2: Each extra unit gives less utility → the consumer will buy additional units only if the price falls → lower prices are associated with larger quantities demanded → the demand curve slopes downward.

column1: According to the theory of consumer behaviour, how do consumers arrange their purchases of different goods?
column2: In a way that maximises the total utility they derive. Marginal utility is the basic building block of this theory.

column1: How do the substitution and income effects relate to the total effect of a price change on quantity demanded?
column2: The total effect of a price change (a movement along the demand curve) is the sum of the substitution effect and the income effect.

column1: Explain the substitution effect of a fall in a good's price.
column2: Price ↓ → the good is now cheaper relative to alternatives → the consumer substitutes towards it (buys more) → quantity demanded ↑. The substitution effect always gives a negative price–quantity relationship.

column1: What is real income (purchasing power)?
column2: The quantity of goods and services a sum of money can buy. It rises when prices fall and falls when prices rise, even if money income is unchanged.

column1: Explain the income effect of a fall in the price of a normal good.
column2: Price ↓ → consumer's real income (purchasing power) ↑ → consumer can afford and wants more of the normal good → quantity demanded ↑.

column1: For a normal good, how do the substitution and income effects of a price fall combine?
column2: They reinforce each other: both increase quantity demanded, which explains the downward-sloping demand curve.

column1: For most goods, is the substitution effect or the income effect more important in explaining the law of demand? Why?
column2: The substitution effect. Most goods cost a small fraction of income, so a price change has only a tiny effect on real income. The income effect matters only for goods that take up a large share of income.

column1: What is the supply of an individual firm?
column2: The various quantities of a good or service a firm is willing and able to produce and supply to the market for sale at different possible prices, during a particular time period, ceteris paribus.

column1: Who are the sellers (suppliers) in product markets and in resource markets?
column2:
Product markets: firms sell goods and services.
Resource markets: households sell factors of production.

column1: What is a supply schedule?
column2: A table showing the various quantities of a good that a firm (or the market) is willing and able to produce and supply at various prices.

column1: State the law of supply.
column2: There is a positive relationship between the quantity of a good supplied over a particular time period and its price, ceteris paribus: price ↑ → quantity supplied ↑; price ↓ → quantity supplied ↓.

column1: Why is the relationship described by the law of supply called both 'positive' and 'causal'?
column2: Positive (direct): price and quantity supplied move in the same direction. Causal: changes in price cause the changes in quantity supplied.

column1: Describe a supply curve diagram (axes and slope).
column2: Price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis. The supply curve slopes upward from left to right, showing the positive relationship between price and quantity supplied.

column1: Does a supply curve tell us how much a firm will actually sell and at what price?
column2: No. It shows only how much the firm would be prepared to produce and sell at each possible price; the actual outcome depends on the interaction of supply with demand.

column1: What does a vertical supply curve show?
column2: Quantity supplied is fixed and independent of price: even if price rises, quantity supplied cannot increase.

column1: Why is the supply curve of theatre tickets for a single show vertical?
column2: The quantity is fixed by the number of seats and there is no time to produce more, so quantity supplied cannot rise however high the price.

column1: Why is the supply curve of original Stradivarius violins (or original paintings by famous artists) vertical?
column2: No more originals can ever be produced (reproductions are possible, originals are not), so quantity supplied cannot respond to price.

column1: What is market supply?
column2: The total quantities of a good that all firms are willing and able to supply in a market at different possible prices: the sum of all individual firms' supplies.

column1: How is the market supply curve derived from individual firms' supply curves?
column2: At each possible price, add up the quantities supplied by every firm (horizontal summation). Plotting these totals at every price gives the upward-sloping market supply curve.

column1: What are the non-price determinants of supply?
column2: The factors other than price that influence supply (e.g. factor costs, technology, prices of related goods, taxes, subsidies, number of firms). Changes in them shift the supply curve.

column1: On a supply diagram, what does a rightward shift of the supply curve show, and what is it called?
column2: More is supplied at every given price. It is called an increase in supply.

column1: On a supply diagram, what does a leftward shift of the supply curve show, and what is it called?
column2: Less is supplied at every given price. It is called a decrease in supply.

column1: How does a rise in the price of a factor of production (e.g. wages) affect a firm's supply?
column2: Factor price ↑ → costs of production ↑ → production less profitable → firm produces less → supply ↓ → supply curve shifts left. (Factor price ↓ → shifts right.)

column1: How does an improvement in technology affect supply?
column2: Better technology → costs of production ↓ → production more profitable → supply ↑ → supply curve shifts right. (A less productive technology would shift it left.)

column1: What is competitive supply? Give an example.
column2: Production of one good or another, where the goods compete for the same resources, so producing more of one means producing less of the other (e.g. a farmer choosing to grow wheat or corn).

column1: A farmer can grow wheat or corn. The price of corn rises. What happens to the supply of wheat?
column2: Competitive supply: price of corn ↑ → corn more profitable → farmer switches resources to corn → supply of wheat ↓ → wheat supply curve shifts left. (Price of corn ↓ → wheat supply shifts right.)

column1: What is joint supply? Give an example.
column2: Production of goods derived from a single product, so more of one cannot be produced without producing more of the other (e.g. butter and skimmed milk from whole milk; petrol, diesel and heating oil from crude oil).

column1: Butter and skimmed milk are in joint supply. The price of butter rises. What happens to the supply of skimmed milk?
column2: Price of butter ↑ → quantity of butter supplied ↑ → more whole milk is processed → supply of skimmed milk ↑ → its supply curve shifts right.

column1: Firms expect the price of their product to rise in future. How does this affect current supply?
column2: Expected future price ↑ → firms withhold some current output to sell later at the higher price → current supply ↓ → supply curve shifts left. (Expected price fall → current supply ↑ → shifts right.)

column1: How does a new or higher tax (indirect tax or tax on profits) affect a firm's supply?
column2: Firms treat taxes like costs of production: tax ↑ → costs ↑ → supply ↓ → supply curve shifts left. Removing or cutting a tax → supply curve shifts right.

column1: What is a subsidy (to producers)?
column2: A payment made by the government to a firm, e.g. to raise producers' incomes or to encourage more production of the good. It has the opposite effect to a tax.

column1: How does the introduction of a subsidy affect supply?
column2: Subsidy ↑ → equivalent to a fall in production costs → supply ↑ → supply curve shifts right. Removing or cutting a subsidy → supply curve shifts left.

column1: How does a change in the number of firms affect market supply?
column2: Number of firms ↑ → market supply ↑ → supply curve shifts right (and vice versa), because market supply is the sum of all individual supplies.

column1: What are supply 'shocks'? Give an example.
column2: Sudden, unpredictable events that affect supply, e.g. weather (for farm products), war, natural or man-made disasters such as the 2010 Louisiana (Gulf of Mexico) oil spill, which cut the supply of local seafood.

column1: Distinguish between a 'change in quantity supplied' and a 'change in supply'.
column2:
Change in quantity supplied: caused only by a change in the good's own price; a movement along the supply curve.
Change in supply: caused by a change in a non-price determinant; a shift of the whole supply curve.

column1: A good's price rises, ceteris paribus. Describe what happens on its supply diagram and name the change.
column2: A movement up along the same supply curve (e.g. point A to point B) to a larger quantity. This is an increase in quantity supplied; the curve does not shift.

column1: The price of a key input (e.g. oil) rises. Describe what happens on the product's supply diagram and name the change.
column2: The whole supply curve shifts left (e.g. S1 to S3): less is supplied at every price. This is a decrease in supply.

column1: In microeconomics, what is the short run?
column2: A time period during which at least one input is fixed (unchanging in quantity and quality), e.g. buildings, factories and heavy machinery, while other inputs such as labour and materials are variable.

column1: In microeconomics, what is the long run?
column2: A time period in which all inputs can be changed: the firm has no fixed inputs.

column1: Do the short run and the long run correspond to particular lengths of time?
column2: No. Some industries can change their fixed inputs within weeks or months, while others take many years.

column1: Distinguish between total product and marginal product.
column2:
Total product: the total quantity of output a firm produces.
Marginal product: the extra output produced by one additional unit of a variable input (e.g. one more worker).

column1: State the law of diminishing marginal returns.
column2: As more and more units of a variable input (e.g. labour) are added to one or more fixed inputs (e.g. land), the marginal product of the variable input at first increases, but eventually begins to decrease. Fixed inputs and technology are held constant.

column1: Why does marginal product at first increase as workers are added to a farm of fixed size?
column2: One worker alone must do every task (ploughing, planting, harvesting), so output is low; additional workers share and divide the work, so each adds more output than the one before.

column1: Why do diminishing marginal returns eventually set in?
column2: Overcrowding of the fixed input: each additional worker has less land (or fewer machines) to work with, so adds less and less output, eventually none.

column1: Why does the law of diminishing marginal returns hold only in the short run?
column2: It requires at least one fixed input. In the long run all inputs can be varied, so no input is fixed.

column1: What would be implied if diminishing marginal returns did not exist?
column2: Output (e.g. food) could be increased indefinitely just by adding variable inputs to a fixed piece of land, which is clearly impossible.

column1: What did David Ricardo predict about agricultural output, and which concept was it based on?
column2: That agricultural output would eventually stop growing, because adding more labour and capital to a fixed quantity of land gives smaller and smaller additions to output: diminishing marginal returns.

column1: Why has world agricultural output kept growing despite a fixed quantity of land (contrary to Ricardo's fears)?
column2: The law of diminishing returns assumes unchanging technology. Technological change (better seeds, fertilisers, machinery, methods) raises the output obtainable from the same land.

column1: What is total cost?
column2: All the costs of production incurred by a firm.

column1: What is marginal cost?
column2: The extra cost of producing one more unit of output: how much total cost increases when output rises by one unit.

column1: How is the pattern of marginal cost related to the pattern of marginal product?
column2: It is the opposite, and determined entirely by diminishing marginal returns: MP rising → MC falling; MP at its maximum → MC at its minimum; MP falling → MC rising.

column1: Why does marginal cost fall at low levels of output?
column2: Marginal product of labour ↑ → each extra worker (who adds to costs) produces more and more output → cost of each additional unit of output ↓.

column1: Why does marginal cost rise once diminishing marginal returns set in?
column2: Marginal product ↓ → each extra worker adds less output → the cost of each additional unit of output (marginal cost) ↑.

column1: How is a firm's supply curve related to its marginal cost curve?
column2: The supply curve is a portion of the upward-sloping marginal cost curve: it shows the price–quantity combinations where the marginal cost of producing one more unit equals the price of that unit.

column1: How does increasing marginal cost explain the upward-sloping supply curve?
column2: Diminishing returns → marginal cost ↑ as output ↑ → firm will produce extra units only if the price rises to cover the extra cost of each extra unit → higher price needed for a larger quantity supplied.

column1: Where on the marginal cost curve does a firm's supply curve begin?
column2: At the point where the firm earns enough revenue to be better off producing than shutting down (where it covers all its variable costs); the supply curve is the upward-sloping part of MC above that point.

column1: What is excess supply (a surplus)?
column2: A situation where, at a given price, quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. It occurs at prices above the equilibrium price.

column1: What is excess demand (a shortage)?
column2: A situation where, at a given price, quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. It occurs at prices below the equilibrium price.

column1: On a demand and supply diagram, how is the size of a shortage or surplus at a given price shown?
column2: As the horizontal distance between the demand curve and the supply curve at that price.

column1: In a free market, how is a surplus (excess supply) eliminated?
column2: Unsold output → producers lower the price → quantity demanded ↑ and quantity supplied ↓ → downward pressure on price continues until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied and the surplus disappears.

column1: In a free market, how is a shortage (excess demand) eliminated?
column2: Goods sell out quickly → producers raise the price → quantity demanded ↓ and quantity supplied ↑ → upward pressure on price continues until the shortage disappears.

column1: In economics, what is equilibrium?
column2: A state of balance between different forces, such that there is no tendency to change.

column1: What is market equilibrium?
column2: The situation where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: the forces of demand and supply are in balance and there is no tendency for the price to change.

column1: How are equilibrium price and quantity shown on a demand and supply diagram?
column2: At the intersection of the demand and supply curves: read across to the vertical axis for the equilibrium (market) price and down to the horizontal axis for the equilibrium quantity.

column1: What is market disequilibrium?
column2: A situation at any price other than the equilibrium price, where there is excess demand (a shortage) or excess supply (a surplus).

column1: Why can't a market disequilibrium last in a free competitive market?
column2: The forces of demand and supply push the price to change (up when there is a shortage, down when there is a surplus) until it reaches its equilibrium level.

column1: Once a competitive market is in equilibrium, what can cause the equilibrium to change?
column2: Only a change in a non-price determinant of demand or supply, which shifts a curve; the market then adjusts to a new equilibrium.

column1: Consumer incomes rise and the good is normal. Explain how the market moves to a new equilibrium.
column2: Demand shifts right → at the original price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (shortage) → upward pressure on price → price ↑, moving up the supply curve until the shortage is eliminated → new equilibrium with a higher price and higher quantity.

column1: The number of consumers falls. Explain how the market moves to a new equilibrium.
column2: Demand shifts left → at the original price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (surplus) → downward pressure on price → price ↓, moving down the supply curve until the surplus is eliminated → new equilibrium with a lower price and lower quantity.

column1: An improvement in technology increases supply. Explain how the market moves to a new equilibrium.
column2: Supply shifts right → at the original price there is a surplus → price falls, moving down the demand curve until the surplus is eliminated → new equilibrium with a lower price and higher quantity.

column1: The number of firms in an industry falls. Explain how the market moves to a new equilibrium.
column2: Supply shifts left → at the original price there is a shortage → price rises, moving up the demand curve until the shortage is eliminated → new equilibrium with a higher price and lower quantity.

column1: Diagram: the demand curve shifts right while supply is unchanged. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
column2: Both rise: the new intersection is further up the supply curve (higher P, higher Q).

column1: Diagram: the demand curve shifts left while supply is unchanged. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
column2: Both fall: the new intersection is further down the supply curve (lower P, lower Q).

column1: Diagram: the supply curve shifts right while demand is unchanged. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
column2: Price falls and quantity rises: the new intersection is further down the demand curve.

column1: Diagram: the supply curve shifts left while demand is unchanged. What happens to equilibrium price and quantity?
column2: Price rises and quantity falls: the new intersection is further up the demand curve.

column1: Science showed that avocados are rich in healthy fats. Using demand and supply, explain what happened to avocado prices.
column2: Tastes changed in favour of avocados → demand shifts right → shortage at the old price → price ↑ → new equilibrium with a higher price and quantity (world consumption and prices rose).

column1: The very hot UK summer of 2018 cut potato crops by about one-third. Using demand and supply, explain the effect on the price of potato chips (crisps).
column2: Weather shock → fewer, dearer potatoes (a key input) → supply of chips shifts left → shortage at the old price → price of chips ↑ and quantity ↓.

column1: Distinguish between free goods and economic goods in terms of scarcity and opportunity cost.
column2:
Free goods: not scarce; zero opportunity cost.
Economic goods: scarce; opportunity cost greater than zero.

column1: Using demand and supply, define a free good.
column2: A good for which quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded at a zero price: supply is so large relative to demand that there is excess quantity supplied even when the price is zero.

column1: Using demand and supply, define an economic good.
column2: A good for which quantity supplied is smaller than quantity demanded at a zero price, so demand and supply intersect at a price above zero.

column1: How can a free good become an economic good? Describe the curve shifts.
column2: A leftward shift of supply (reduced supply) and/or a rightward shift of demand (increased demand) until the curves intersect at a price above zero.

column1: What is the price mechanism?
column2: The system in which prices, determined by the forces of demand and supply in competitive markets, allocate resources and ration goods.

column1: In a market economy, how is the 'what/how much to produce' question of resource allocation answered?
column2: Through prices in free markets: firms produce only the goods consumers are willing and able to buy, and consumers buy only the goods producers are willing and able to supply.

column1: In a market economy, how is the 'how to produce' question of resource allocation answered?
column2: Through prices: firms use the resources and technologies in production that they are willing and able to pay for.

column1: What is the 'invisible hand' of the market?
column2: Adam Smith's phrase for the market mechanism working through prices, which coordinates the buying and selling decisions of millions of decision-makers without any central authority.

column1: What is the signalling function of prices?
column2: Prices communicate information to decision-makers, e.g. a rising price signals to producers that a shortage has emerged.

column1: What is the incentive function of prices?
column2: Prices motivate decision-makers to respond to the information they convey, e.g. a higher price motivates producers to supply more (it is more profitable) and consumers to buy less.

column1: Consumers want more strawberries because of their health benefits. Explain how price signals and incentives reallocate resources.
column2: Demand ↑ → shortage at the old price → price ↑ → signals the shortage to producers and gives them an incentive to supply more (movement up S) → higher price also signals consumers to buy less than they would at the old price (movement along new D) → more resources allocated to strawberries (answers 'what to produce').

column1: Immigration increases the supply of labour. Explain how the wage acts as a signal and incentive that reallocates resources.
column2: Labour supply ↑ → surplus of labour at the old wage → wage ↓ → signals the surplus to firms and gives them an incentive to hire more labour (movement down D) → lower wage signals workers to offer less labour (movement along new S) → firms produce with more labour (answers 'how to produce').

column1: Why does the demand curve for labour slope downward and the supply curve of labour slope upward?
column2:
Demand: as the wage falls, firms are prompted to hire more labour.
Supply: the higher the wage, the more willing workers are to supply their labour.

column1: What is rationing?
column2: A method of apportioning (parcelling out) goods and services among consumers or households.

column1: What is price rationing?
column2: Allocating goods by prices freely determined in markets: everyone willing and able to pay the price gets the good, and those not willing or able to pay do not. Price alone decides.

column1: Why does price rationing at the equilibrium price satisfy all buyers and sellers?
column2: At the market-determined equilibrium price and quantity, the buying and selling choices of all buyers and sellers in the market are satisfied and in balance.

column1: When do non-price rationing systems come into play?
column2: When the price mechanism is not working properly, e.g. in planned economies or when governments impose price controls.

column1: What is the most common non-price rationing method?
column2: The waiting line (queue), where consumers get the good on a first come, first served basis.

column1: Distinguish between price rationing and non-price rationing.
column2:
Price rationing: goods go to those willing and able to pay the market price.
Non-price rationing: goods are apportioned by other means (e.g. queues) when prices are not allowed to do the job.

column1: What is marginal benefit?
column2: The extra benefit (satisfaction) a consumer gets from consuming one more unit of a good. It falls as more units are consumed.

column1: Why can the demand curve also be called a marginal benefit (MB) curve?
column2: It shows what consumers are willing to pay for one more unit. Since marginal benefit falls as quantity consumed rises, consumers buy an extra unit only if its price falls.

column1: Distinguish between marginal utility and marginal benefit.
column2:
Marginal utility: extra satisfaction from one more unit; it cannot actually be measured.
Marginal benefit: interpreted as the consumer's willingness to pay for the last unit bought (its price), so it is measurable.

column1: Why can the supply curve also be called a marginal cost (MC) curve?
column2: It shows the price firms are willing to accept to produce one more unit. Since marginal cost rises as output rises, firms produce an extra unit only if its price rises.

column1: Define consumer surplus.
column2: The highest price consumers are willing to pay for a good minus the price they actually pay.

column1: Where is consumer surplus shown on a demand and supply diagram?
column2: The area under the demand curve and above the price paid, up to the quantity purchased.

column1: What does consumer surplus represent?
column2: The extra benefit consumers receive over and above what they pay: many consumers were willing to pay more than the market price but got the good for less.

column1: Define producer surplus.
column2: The price firms receive for selling a good minus the lowest price they are willing to accept to produce it.

column1: Where is producer surplus shown on a demand and supply diagram?
column2: The area above the supply curve and below the price received, up to the quantity produced and sold.

column1: What does producer surplus represent?
column2: The benefit firms gain over and above the lowest price they would have accepted: firms willing to supply at lower prices actually received the higher market price.

column1: What is social surplus (community surplus)?
column2: The sum of consumer surplus and producer surplus.

column1: Why are consumer and producer surplus expressed in money terms?
column2: They measure the monetary value of the benefit gained by consumers and producers.

column1: 'Surplus' is used in two senses in microeconomics. What are they, and how can you tell them apart?
column2: (1) Excess supply (quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded). (2) Benefits gained by consumers and producers (consumer, producer, social surplus). Used on its own, 'surplus' means excess supply.

column1: Describe a diagram showing maximum social surplus at competitive market equilibrium.
column2: D (MB) slopes down and S (MC) slopes up, intersecting at Pe and Qe. Consumer surplus: area between D and the price line Pe, up to Qe. Producer surplus: area between Pe and S, up to Qe. Together, the whole area between D and S up to Qe is social surplus, which is maximum.

column1: Why is social surplus smaller if less than the equilibrium quantity is produced?
column2: Social surplus is then only the area between the demand and supply curves up to the smaller output, so the area between the curves from that output to Qe is lost.

column1: Broadly, what does efficiency mean in economics?
column2: Making the best possible use of scarce resources.

column1: What is allocative efficiency?
column2: Producing the quantity of goods mostly wanted by society: resources are allocated so that society gets the most benefit from consumption. It answers the 'what/how much to produce' question in the best possible way.

column1: What does MB = MC mean at competitive market equilibrium?
column2: The extra benefit to society of one more unit equals the extra cost to society of producing it, so society allocates the 'right' amount of resources to the good and produces the quantity it most wants: allocative efficiency.

column1: If marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost for the last unit produced, what should happen to output, and why?
column2: Output should increase: society values the last unit more than it costs to produce.

column1: If marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit for the last unit produced, what should happen to output, and why?
column2: Output should decrease: the last unit costs society more to produce than the value society places on it.

column1: For allocative efficiency to be achieved in an entire economy, what condition must hold?
column2: MB = MC must hold in all markets.

column1: What are the two equivalent conditions for allocative efficiency at competitive market equilibrium?
column2: (1) Marginal benefit equals marginal cost (MB = MC). (2) Social surplus (consumer plus producer surplus) is at its maximum.

column1: In economics, what does 'welfare' refer to, and when is social welfare at its maximum?
column2: Welfare is the amount of consumer and producer surplus. Social welfare is maximised when social surplus is maximum, i.e. where MB = MC in competitive markets.

column1: What was Adam Smith's idea about self-interest, markets and society's interest?
column2: Individuals acting in their own self-interest will, through the workings of markets, produce an outcome in society's best interest: markets coordinate countless decisions without central authority while promoting the best allocation of scarce resources.

column1: What is welfare loss (deadweight loss)?
column2: The loss of social surplus that occurs when markets fail to achieve allocative efficiency, so social welfare is no longer at its maximum.

column1: How does market failure call into question the idea that governments should not intervene in markets?
column2: Competitive market efficiency needs very strict, unrealistic conditions that are practically never met, so real markets fail to achieve allocative efficiency (welfare loss), which justifies government intervention.

column1: How does income distribution call into question the idea that governments should not intervene in markets?
column2: The competitive market cannot give a satisfactory answer to the 'for whom to produce' question (distribution of output and income), which invites government intervention.

column1: If competitive markets are rare in reality, why is the competitive market model still useful for assessing outcomes and policies?
column2: It provides a standard of economic efficiency against which real, less-than-efficient outcomes can be judged, and against which government policies can be assessed for their efficiency consequences.

column1: How does the competitive market model guide government policy design?
column2: It forms the basis for policies that try to create real-world conditions that allow economies to come closer to achieving economic efficiency.

column1: What is the assumption of rational self-interest (rational economic decision-making)?
column2: Individuals act in their best self-interest, trying to maximise the satisfaction they expect to receive from their economic decisions.

column1: Under the assumption of rational self-interest, what are consumers, firms, workers and investors each assumed to maximise?
column2:
Consumers: satisfaction (utility) from purchases.
Firms: profit.
Workers: wages.
Investors: returns on investments.

column1: What is the completeness assumption of rational consumer choice?
column2: The consumer can rank any two goods (or groups of goods) A and B with certainty: she prefers A to B, prefers B to A, or is indifferent between them.

column1: What is the transitivity assumption of rational consumer choice?
column2: Preferences are consistent: if the consumer prefers A to B, and B to C, she must prefer A to C.

column1: What is the non-satiation assumption of rational consumer choice?
column2: The consumer always prefers more of a good to less.

column1: What does the assumption of perfect information mean in the theory of consumer behaviour?
column2: Consumers have complete knowledge of all their alternatives (all possible products, product qualities and prices), so there is no uncertainty about what they choose.

column1: What does utility maximisation mean?
column2: Consumers make their utility as large as possible by buying the combination of goods and services that gives the greatest total utility for a given amount of money spent (their budget or income).

column1: Which assumptions does the idea of utility maximisation rest on?
column2: Consumer rationality (completeness, transitivity and non-satiation of preferences) and perfect information.

column1: What is behavioural economics?
column2: A branch of economics, influenced mainly by psychology (also sociology and neuroscience), based on the idea that human behaviour is far more complex than consumer rationality assumes. It began to flourish around the start of the 21st century.

column1: How does behavioural economics study decision-making differently from the standard theory of consumer behaviour?
column2: The standard theory relies on assumptions about human behaviour; behavioural economics relies extensively on experiments that observe how people actually behave and react in different situations.

column1: What is a bias (cognitive bias)?
column2: A term from psychology for a systematic error in thinking or evaluating: a departure from normal standards of thought or judgement.

column1: What is a rule of thumb (as a consumer bias)? Give an example.
column2: A simple guideline based on experience and common sense that simplifies a complicated decision, e.g. 'one serving of fruit is the size of a fist' or 'a portion of salad is two handfuls'.

column1: Why do rules of thumb conflict with the assumption of consumer rationality?
column2: Rational choice requires complex consideration of every possible alternative; rules of thumb replace measurement and calculation with simple shortcuts, so choices need not maximise utility.

column1: What is anchoring? Give an example.
column2: Using irrelevant information to make a decision, often simply the first piece of information encountered, e.g. seeing jeans at $150 makes a similar $100 pair seem a bargain, though the same jeans sell for $50 elsewhere.

column1: What is framing? Give an example.
column2: The way choices are presented (framed) affects decisions, e.g. consumers prefer beef described as '80% lean' to beef described as '20% fat', although the information is identical.

column1: Give an example of a purchase framed by the seller's environment rather than by language.
column2: Consumers may pay more for a faded pair of jeans in a boutique than for an identical pair in a discount store.

column1: Why would a perfectly rational consumer be unaffected by framing?
column2: The information is exactly the same, only presented differently, so a rational consumer would be indifferent between the two presentations.

column1: What is the availability bias? Give an example.
column2: Relying more heavily on the most recently available information (because it is remembered more easily), though it is no more reliable than older information, e.g. choosing a brand after recently seeing a lot of advertising for it.

column1: What is bounded rationality?
column2: Herbert Simon's idea that consumers are rational only within limits, because of insufficient information, the cost of obtaining information, and the limited capacity of the human mind to process large amounts of information.

column1: In behavioural economics, what does it mean to 'satisfice'?
column2: To seek a satisfactory outcome rather than an optimal (best) one. Simon argued consumers satisfice rather than maximise.

column1: Which economist developed the idea of bounded rationality, and what argument was it based on?
column2: Herbert Simon (Nobel Prize winner for work on economic decision-making): people have a limited capacity to process information, and searching for the information needed to maximise utility is itself costly.

column1: What is bounded self-control? Give an example.
column2: The idea that people exercise self-control only within limits, so they often lack the self-control rational decisions require, e.g. eating or spending too much, saving or working too little.

column1: What is bounded selfishness?
column2: The idea that people are selfish only within limits: self-interested maximisation cannot explain the many cases of selfless behaviour and willingness to contribute to the public good at a cost to personal welfare.

column1: How does imperfect information undermine the assumption of utility maximisation?
column2: Consumers do not and cannot have full information on prices, products and product quality, so they choose using faulty and incomplete information and are unable to maximise utility.

column1: Distinguish between bounded rationality, bounded self-control and bounded selfishness.
column2:
Bounded rationality: limited ability to obtain and process information.
Bounded self-control: limited willpower to act on rational decisions.
Bounded selfishness: self-interest is limited; people also act selflessly.

column1: In economics, what is a nudge?
column2: A method designed to influence consumers' choices in a predictable way, without offering financial incentives or imposing sanctions, and without limiting choice.

column1: Who coined the economic term 'nudge', and where?
column2: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, in their 2008 book 'Nudge: Improving Decisions about Health, Wealth and Happiness'. Thaler received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Economics partly for his work on behavioural economics.

column1: What is the aim of nudges?
column2: To influence people to behave in socially desirable ways without imposing any constraints on their behaviour, so freedom of choice is maintained.

column1: Who uses nudges in practice?
column2: Governments in many countries (some have set up 'nudge units' for public policy) and the private sector.

column1: Give an example of a nudge using social norms to raise tax payments.
column2: In the UK, payments by late taxpayers rose 15% when they were told most people in their area had already paid: they were made to feel the exception to the community norm.

column1: Give an example of a nudge used to reduce household electricity consumption.
column2: In a Danish municipality, streetlights turn red when solar panels can no longer power them, making residents more aware of their electricity use.

column1: Give an example of a nudge used to promote healthy eating.
column2: Placing healthy foods in more visible and accessible positions in stores (and painting colourful footsteps leading to them) has increased their sales.

column1: How did personalised messages work as a nudge for vehicle tax non-payers?
column2: Personalised messages instead of warning letters doubled the number of payers; adding a photo of the car tripled it.

column1: How did the design of tax notices act as a nudge?
column2: Sending notices in white rather than brown envelopes, with handwritten rather than typed names, increased the number of people paying their tax by 16%.

column1: In which field has behavioural economics been most successful, and where else is it making headway?
column2: Most successful in finance; also making headway in development, health, law and economics, public economics, organisational economics and wage determination.

column1: What is 'libertarian paternalism'?
column2: Thaler and Sunstein's description of nudges as government intervention: steering people towards choices judged to be in their best interests (paternalism) while preserving their freedom of choice (libertarian).

column1: What is choice architecture?
column2: The design of the ways or environments in which people make choices, based on the idea that decisions are influenced by the context and by how options are presented.

column1: Who are choice architects?
column2: Individuals or organisations that arrange the context in which choices are made.

column1: Why is framing an important part of choice architecture?
column2: Framing defines the context in which choices are presented to decision-makers, so it is used to influence their decisions.

column1: What is a default choice, and why can it be used as a nudge?
column2: The option that results if a person does nothing. People often stick with defaults out of habit, lack of interest or comfort in not choosing, so making an option the default induces people to follow it.

column1: How does default choice affect organ donation rates?
column2: Where being a donor is the default (e.g. Austria, Belgium, France), participation is very high, sometimes 90% or more; where being a non-donor is the default (e.g. Denmark, Germany, the US), it is much lower.

column1: What is a restricted choice? Give examples.
column2: A choice limited by the government or another authority, e.g. speed limits, voting age, recycling regulations, smoking prohibitions (or social norms).

column1: Why is it argued that restricted choices are necessary?
column2: People have too many choices and, lacking good information or through poor judgement, often choose badly; restrictions encourage choices with socially desirable outcomes.

column1: What is a mandated choice?
column2: A choice between alternatives that the government or another authority makes compulsory: the choice itself is free, but making it is required.

column1: Give an example of mandated choice and its effect.
column2: In Illinois (US), renewing a driver's licence requires answering whether you wish to be an organ donor: 60% sign up, compared with 38% nationally where the choice is not mandated.

column1: How did an organ donation nudge backfire in the Netherlands?
column2: A 2016 law made being a donor the default, but in a drive soon after there were six times as many non-donors as donors, probably because people (after heavy press coverage) rebelled against the government choosing for them.

column1: What do default, restricted and mandated choice have in common?
column2: They are different types of nudge within choice architecture, intended to steer people's choices in a direction held to be socially desirable.

column1: How do mainstream economists defend the rational theory of consumer behaviour against behavioural critiques?
column2: It explains and predicts behaviour reasonably well: consumers do respond rationally to monetary factors (e.g. a higher petrol tax lowers quantity demanded) and many tests confirm downward-sloping demand curves, so on average behaviour fits utility theory.

column1: Why do some economists argue that choice architecture and nudges are manipulative?
column2: They try to control consumer choices, often at a subconscious level, by exploiting incomplete information and selectively providing information, so free choice becomes an illusion.

column1: What safeguard is proposed for the use of nudges in economic policy?
column2: Transparency and open discussion of the nudges being used.

column1: Evaluation: what is the cost advantage of policies based on behavioural economics?
column2: They may be a relatively simple and low-cost way to influence people to act in socially desirable ways.

column1: Evaluation: what does the past success of nudges suggest about their potential?
column2: Nudges and choice architecture have worked in a number of areas, suggesting many possible applications in areas not yet explored.

column1: Evaluation: how do nudges compare with other policies in terms of freedom of choice?
column2: They preserve freedom of choice: people are not forced to do anything or prevented from doing anything.

column1: Evaluation: what advantage does behavioural economics have over the standard theory of consumer behaviour?
column2: It may be able to explain the inconsistencies and seeming irrationality of actual consumer behaviour that the standard theory cannot.

column1: Evaluation: why does the psychological basis of behavioural policies count as an advantage?
column2: They draw on principles of psychology, such as framing, many of which have been tested over many years.

column1: Evaluation: what is the advantage of behavioural policies being developed through trials?
column2: Trials give a flexible trial-and-error way of discovering policy measures that actually achieve the desired results.

column1: Evaluation: why is the lack of a unifying theory a weakness of behavioural economics?
column2: Its body of knowledge is not based on an understanding of human behaviour, so it cannot produce a systematic theory of consumer behaviour with general applicability.

column1: Evaluation: why might behavioural policies fail to work across time, groups or cultures?
column2: The unsystematic approach (different policies for different situations) may not hold over time or across income, social or cultural groups, which limits the policies' applicability.

column1: Evaluation: how could the psychological principles behind nudges be misused?
column2: To manipulate consumers into acting against their best interests, as advertising and marketing have long done (e.g. advertising unhealthy sugary and fatty foods).

column1: Evaluation: why is there a risk in governments using nudges instead of traditional policies?
column2: Nudges may be used as substitutes for necessary but politically costly policies, such as taxes on demerit goods or on goods causing negative externalities, and traditional policies (indirect taxes, subsidies) may be more effective.

column1: Evaluation: why might nudging be a dangerous 'camouflaged' form of regulation?
column2: It may be government regulation disguised as freedom of choice, so people may not be aware of it or of its effects on their choices.

column1: Evaluation: even when nudges successfully change choices, what is the remaining concern?
column2: The choices people make may not reflect their true preferences.

column1: What is profit maximisation as a business objective?
column2: The standard assumption of rational producer behaviour: the firm chooses the level of output that makes profit as large as possible.

column1: In general terms, what is a firm's profit?
column2: The total revenue earned by the firm minus the total costs it incurs in producing its output.

column1: What is the common theme of theories of alternative business objectives?
column2: Profit maximisation may not be the overriding objective of firms: they may have other goals that are more important.

column1: Give examples of firm behaviour where self-interest conflicts with the well-being of society.
column2: Polluting the environment; employing poorly paid children forced to work long hours; using labour in unhealthy or dangerous conditions (where laws protecting workers are missing or poorly enforced).

column1: What is corporate social responsibility (CSR)?
column2: Firms engaging in socially beneficial activities, e.g. avoiding pollution, environmentally sound practices, supporting human rights (avoiding exploited or child labour), arts and sports sponsorships, donations to charity.

column1: How can a negative public image give firms an incentive to adopt corporate social responsibility?
column2: Unethical behaviour → negative image among workers and buyers → lower worker productivity, lost sales and even boycotts → lower revenue and profit.

column1: How can corporate social responsibility affect the government regulation a firm faces?
column2: Socially irresponsible behaviour → government regulation to limit the harm to society; socially responsible behaviour → less government regulation.

column1: What has driven the growth of corporate social responsibility practices?
column2: Greater consumer awareness and concern about the social, ethical and environmental aspects of business, consumer activism (boycotts), and rapidly growing interest in investing in firms that meet social, ethical and ecological criteria.

column1: Does corporate social responsibility reduce firms' profits?
column2: Economists used to think so, looking only at costs (e.g. cheap child labour lowers costs). But profit also depends on revenue, which falls if consumers shun offending firms. Studies are inconclusive, but firms often avoid risking consumer displeasure.

column1: What is market share?
column2: The percentage of total sales in a market that is earned by a single firm.

column1: Why is a large market share likely to increase a firm's profitability?
column2: A large market share means the firm is probably achieving economies of scale (falling costs per unit of output as it grows).

column1: Why is market share used as a key indicator of a firm's performance?
column2: It shows how well the firm is doing relative to its competitors; multinational corporations often measure their performance by market share in specific countries.

column1: What does a stable, growing or falling market share tell a firm?
column2:
Stable: revenues growing at the same rate as the market.
Growing: doing better than competitors (revenues growing faster).
Falling: doing worse than competitors in sales.

column1: What strategies can a firm use to increase its market share?
column2: Lowering its prices, introducing new or innovative products, and advertising.

column1: Why may pursuing market share lower profits, and when is it still worthwhile?
column2: Lower prices may reduce revenue, while R&D and advertising raise costs. It is worthwhile as long as the firm remains profitable and earns a satisfactory level of profit.

column1: What is growth maximisation as a business objective?
column2: Aiming to maximise the growth (size) of the firm rather than its profits.

column1: How can growth maximisation increase a firm's profitability through lower costs?
column2: A growing firm can achieve economies of scale, lowering its average costs.

column1: How does growth reduce a firm's dependence on a single product or market?
column2: As it grows, the firm can diversify into producing different products for different markets.

column1: How does growth increase a firm's ability to influence prices?
column2: A larger firm has greater market power, which can increase its profitability.

column1: How does growth reduce the risks a firm faces?
column2: A larger firm may be less affected in an economic downturn (recession) and is less likely to be taken over (bought) by another firm.

column1: Why does growth maximisation reconcile the interests of a firm's owners and managers?
column2: Both groups gain from a growing firm, whereas other objectives can set them against each other (owners tend to favour profit maximisation, managers revenue maximisation).

column1: What is revenue maximisation, and why is it linked to the separation of ownership from management?
column2: Aiming to maximise sales revenue. Hired managers (unlike owner-managers) may be more interested in increasing sales and revenue than in maximising profit.

column1: Why are sales targets more practical than profit targets for managing a firm?
column2: Sales can be identified and measured more easily over the short term than profits, and sales targets can be used to motivate employees.

column1: How do reward systems within firms encourage revenue maximisation?
column2: Rewards for managers and employees are often linked to increased sales rather than to increased profits.

column1: Why might maximising revenue also raise profit?
column2: It is often assumed that revenue from extra sales rises faster than costs, in which case profit also increases.

column1: What is satisficing as a business objective?
column2: Herbert Simon's idea that firms aim for a satisfactory level of profit together with satisfactory results on many other objectives, rather than the best result for any one objective.

column1: Why, according to Herbert Simon, can a large modern firm not pursue a single maximising objective?
column2: It is made up of many separate groups with their own overlapping or conflicting objectives, so it reaches compromises and pursues many objectives arranged in a hierarchy.

column1: In economics, what is elasticity?
column2: A measure of the responsiveness of a variable to changes in price or in any of the variable's determinants.

column1: What is price elasticity of demand (PED)?
column2: A measure of the responsiveness of the quantity of a good demanded to changes in its price, measured along a given demand curve.

column1: In general terms, distinguish between price elastic and price inelastic demand.
column2:
Price elastic: quantity demanded is highly responsive to a change in price.
Price inelastic: quantity demanded is not very responsive to a change in price.

column1: Why is PED usually a negative number, and how is the sign treated?
column2: Price and quantity demanded are negatively related, so a price rise brings a fall in quantity demanded. By convention the minus sign is dropped (the absolute value is taken) and PED is treated as positive.

column1: Why do economists drop the minus sign from PED?
column2: To avoid confusion when comparing values: treated as positive numbers, a PED of 3 is clearly more elastic than a PED of 2, whereas with signs the more elastic value would look 'smaller'.

column1: Why is elasticity measured with percentage changes rather than changes in units or currency?
column2: Percentages give a measure independent of units, so elasticities can be compared across goods measured in different units (oranges vs cars) and across countries with different currencies.

column1: Why are absolute changes in price (e.g. a $15 rise) meaningless for measuring responsiveness?
column2: The same absolute rise means very different things for a good costing $100 and one costing $5000; percentage changes put responsiveness into perspective.

column1: In what units is price elasticity of demand measured?
column2: None: elasticity is a pure number, not a percentage, and has no units.

column1: When is demand price inelastic, in terms of percentage changes and the value of PED?
column2: When the percentage change in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage change in price: PED is greater than zero but less than one, so quantity demanded is relatively unresponsive to price.

column1: When is demand price elastic, in terms of percentage changes and the value of PED?
column2: When the percentage change in quantity demanded is larger than the percentage change in price: PED is greater than one (but less than infinity), so quantity demanded is relatively responsive to price.

column1: When is demand unit elastic (unitary PED)?
column2: When the percentage change in quantity demanded equals the percentage change in price, so PED equals one.

column1: What is perfectly inelastic demand? Give an example.
column2: Quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes (PED of zero), e.g. a heroin addict's quantity of heroin demanded.

column1: What is perfectly elastic demand?
column2: A change in price causes an infinitely large response in quantity demanded (PED of infinity): at the given price consumers buy any quantity available; if price rises, quantity demanded drops to zero.

column1: What is the possible range of PED values, and what does a larger value indicate?
column2: From zero to infinity. The larger the value, the greater the responsiveness of quantity demanded to price.

column1: Which PED cases are frequently encountered in practice, and which are mainly important in theory?
column2:
Frequent: price inelastic (between 0 and 1) and price elastic (greater than 1).
Rare but important in theory: unit elastic, perfectly inelastic and perfectly elastic demand.

column1: Describe the demand curve for perfectly inelastic demand.
column2: A vertical line at a fixed quantity: quantity demanded stays the same whatever the price (PED of zero along its whole length).

column1: Describe the demand curve for perfectly elastic demand.
column2: A horizontal line at a given price: consumers buy any quantity at that price, and nothing at a higher price (PED of infinity along its whole length).

column1: Describe a unit elastic demand curve.
column2: A curve bowed towards the origin (a rectangular hyperbola) with a PED of one at every point: any percentage price change gives an equal percentage change in quantity.

column1: Which three types of demand curve have a constant PED along their entire length?
column2: Unit elastic (PED of one), perfectly inelastic (vertical, PED of zero) and perfectly elastic (horizontal, PED of infinity).

column1: As a rough guide, how is the steepness of a demand curve related to its PED?
column2: The flatter the demand curve, the more elastic the demand (higher PED); the steeper the curve, the less elastic (lower PED).

column1: Why can't you always compare the PEDs of two demand curves just by looking at their steepness?
column2: Curves drawn on different scales are not comparable: two identical demand curves can look flatter or steeper simply because the axis scales differ.

column1: When is it valid to compare the PEDs of two demand curves by their steepness?
column2: When the curves intersect (or would intersect if drawn on the same diagram): then at any given price the flatter curve is the more elastic.

column1: How does PED vary along a straight-line, downward-sloping demand curve?
column2: Demand is price elastic at high prices and low quantities, unit elastic at the midpoint, and price inelastic at low prices and high quantities: PED falls continuously as you move down the curve.

column1: Why is demand price elastic at high prices on a straight-line demand curve?
column2: At high prices and low quantities, a given change in quantity is a large percentage of the small initial quantity, while the price change is a small percentage of the high initial price, so PED is large.

column1: Why is demand price inelastic at low prices on a straight-line demand curve?
column2: At low prices and high quantities, a given change in quantity is a small percentage of the large initial quantity, while the price change is a large percentage of the low initial price, so PED is small.

column1: Why should 'elastic' and 'inelastic' not be used to describe an entire straight-line demand curve?
column2: PED changes along the curve, so the terms apply only to a portion of it at a particular price or price range (the three constant-PED curves are the exceptions).

column1: Using the slope of the demand curve, explain why PED keeps falling as you move down a straight-line demand curve.
column2: The slope of a straight line is constant, so PED depends only on the ratio of price to quantity; moving down the curve price falls and quantity rises, so that ratio, and therefore PED, gets smaller and smaller.

column1: How does the number of substitutes affect PED?
column2: More substitutes → when price rises consumers can switch to other products → large fall in quantity demanded → more elastic demand. Few or no substitutes → small fall → inelastic demand.

column1: Why is the demand for one brand of toothpaste price elastic, while the demand for petrol is price inelastic?
column2: Toothpaste brands are close substitutes, so consumers switch when one brand's price rises. Petrol has no close substitutes, so a price rise reduces quantity demanded only a little.

column1: How does the closeness of substitutes affect PED?
column2: The closer the substitutes (greater substitutability, e.g. Coca-Cola and Pepsi rather than Coca-Cola and orange juice), the easier it is to switch, so the greater the PED.

column1: How does the breadth of a good's definition affect its PED?
column2: The more narrowly a good is defined, the more close substitutes it has and the more elastic its demand: apples are more elastic than fruit, fruit more than food; a Honda more than cars in general.

column1: How does whether a good is a necessity or a luxury affect its PED?
column2: Necessities (goods we cannot do without) have less elastic demand than luxuries: medications and food are very inelastic, while diamond rings are elastic.

column1: How does addiction affect PED?
column2: Addiction is a special case of necessity: the greater the degree of addiction to a substance (e.g. alcohol, cigarettes), the more inelastic the demand.

column1: How does the length of time consumers have to respond affect PED?
column2: Longer time period → consumers can reconsider whether they want the good and find out about alternatives → demand becomes more elastic.

column1: Why is the demand for heating oil inelastic in the short run but more elastic in the long run?
column2: In the short run consumers can do little to switch heating; over time they can switch to other systems (e.g. gas) or install better insulation.

column1: How does the proportion of income spent on a good affect its PED?
column2: The larger the share of income needed to buy it, the more elastic the demand: the same percentage price rise brings a bigger response for cars than for pens.

column1: A lemonade seller raises her price by 500% for a diabetic boy whose blood sugar is dangerously low, and he still buys. What does this show about PED?
column2: His demand at that moment is extremely price inelastic, because the drink is an urgent necessity with no substitute available. Other children, for whom it is not a necessity, would cut their quantity demanded sharply.

column1: What is total revenue (TR)?
column2: The amount of money a firm receives from selling a good or service: the price of the good multiplied by the quantity sold.

column1: Demand is price elastic. What happens to total revenue when the price rises, and why?
column2: Price ↑ → proportionately larger fall in quantity demanded → the quantity effect outweighs the price effect → TR ↓. Price and TR move in opposite directions.

column1: Demand is price elastic. What happens to total revenue when the price falls, and why?
column2: Price ↓ → proportionately larger rise in quantity demanded → TR ↑.

column1: Demand is price inelastic. What happens to total revenue when the price rises, and why?
column2: Price ↑ → proportionately smaller fall in quantity demanded → the price effect outweighs the quantity effect → TR ↑. Price and TR move in the same direction.

column1: Demand is price inelastic. What happens to total revenue when the price falls, and why?
column2: Price ↓ → proportionately smaller rise in quantity demanded → TR ↓.

column1: Demand is unit elastic. What happens to total revenue when the price changes?
column2: Nothing: the percentage change in quantity exactly offsets the percentage change in price, so total revenue stays constant.

column1: Distinguish between total revenue and profit.
column2:
Total revenue: the money a firm receives from its sales.
Profit: total revenue minus total costs.

column1: How is total revenue shown on a demand curve diagram?
column2: As the rectangle under a point on the demand curve: height equal to the price, width equal to the quantity sold.

column1: Diagram: price rises along an elastic section of a demand curve. Describe the change in the total revenue rectangles.
column2: The firm gains a rectangle from the higher price on the units still sold but loses a larger rectangle from the units no longer sold, so total revenue falls.

column1: Diagram: price rises along an inelastic section of a demand curve. Describe the change in the total revenue rectangles.
column2: The rectangle gained from the higher price on units still sold is larger than the rectangle lost from units no longer sold, so total revenue rises.

column1: Diagram: price changes along a unit elastic demand curve. Describe the change in the total revenue rectangles.
column2: The revenue rectangle gained exactly matches the rectangle lost, so total revenue is unchanged.

column1: A firm wants to increase its total revenue. How should it change its price?
column2: Lower the price if demand is elastic; raise it if demand is inelastic. If demand is unit elastic, a price change cannot change total revenue.

column1: How does PED affect the tax revenue a government receives from an indirect tax?
column2: The lower the PED of the taxed good, the greater the tax revenue: with inelastic demand the tax-induced price rise reduces quantity demanded proportionately less, so more units remain to be taxed.

column1: How does an indirect tax affect the supply curve?
column2: It shifts the supply curve upward (equivalent to a leftward shift) by the amount of the tax per unit, because firms must receive a price higher by the tax for every quantity they supply.

column1: On an indirect tax diagram, how is the government's tax revenue shown?
column2: As the rectangle whose height is the tax per unit (the vertical distance between the two supply curves) and whose width is the after-tax quantity.

column1: Diagram: compare the tax revenue from the same indirect tax when demand is inelastic and when it is elastic.
column2: Inelastic demand: the after-tax quantity falls only a little, so the tax revenue rectangle is large. Elastic demand: quantity falls a lot, so the rectangle (tax revenue) is smaller.

column1: Why are indirect taxes usually imposed on goods such as cigarettes and petrol?
column2: They have a low PED, so taxing them raises a lot of revenue: quantity demanded falls proportionately less than the price rises.

column1: What are primary commodities?
column2: Goods arising directly from natural resources (the factor of production 'land'): agricultural, fishing and forestry products, and products of extractive industries (oil, coal, minerals).

column1: What are manufactured products?
column2: Goods produced by labour usually working with capital and raw materials, e.g. cars, computers, televisions.

column1: Why do many primary commodities have a low PED?
column2: They are necessities with no substitutes (e.g. food, oil, minerals), so quantity demanded responds little to price changes.

column1: Why do manufactured products usually have a higher PED than primary commodities?
column2: Even when they are necessities, they usually have substitutes, so quantity demanded is more responsive to price.

column1: Give an exception to the rule that manufactured products have relatively price elastic demand.
column2: Medications: they are manufactured, but their demand is inelastic because they are necessities with no substitutes.

column1: Roughly what is the estimated PED of food in developed countries?
column2: Between 0.20 and 0.25: highly price inelastic.

column1: What is price volatility?
column2: Large price fluctuations over short periods of time (volatility means instability or high variability).

column1: Diagram: why do supply shifts cause larger price fluctuations for primary commodities than for manufactured products?
column2: With inelastic demand (steep D), a supply shift causes a large change in price and a small change in quantity; with elastic demand (flatter D) the same shift causes a much smaller price change.

column1: Why does the supply of agricultural products shift so often?
column2: Farm output depends on factors beyond farmers' control (drought, pests, floods, frost, other natural disasters, or exceptionally good weather), causing frequent, large supply changes over short periods.

column1: Bad weather causes a poor crop of a commodity with inelastic demand. What happens to farmers' total revenue?
column2: Supply ↓ → price rises by a larger percentage than quantity falls → farmers' total revenue ↑. Ironically, a poor crop may be good for farmers.

column1: An exceptionally good harvest increases the supply of a crop with inelastic demand. What happens to farmers' total revenue?
column2: Supply ↑ → price falls by a larger percentage than quantity rises → farmers' total revenue ↓. Ironically, a good crop may be bad for farmers.

column1: How does the price volatility of primary commodities affect their producers?
column2: Producers' incomes depend on their revenues from sales, so they fluctuate widely along with commodity prices.

column1: What is the link between unstable farm revenues and government intervention in agriculture?
column2: Unstable farmer revenues are an important reason why governments intervene to support farmers' incomes.

column1: Give examples of goods with price inelastic demand and goods with price elastic demand.
column2:
Price inelastic: petrol, cigarettes, food.
Price elastic: yachts, expensive holidays.

column1: What is income elasticity of demand (YED)?
column2: A measure of the responsiveness of demand to changes in income. It involves shifts of the demand curve.

column1: What two pieces of information does YED give about demand?
column2: The direction of the change in demand when income changes (from its sign) and the size of the change, i.e. how far the demand curve shifts (from its value).

column1: Distinguish between what PED and YED show on a demand diagram.
column2:
