column2: High barriers to entry let firms enjoy the profits from their inventions, new products and technologies, which gives an incentive to innovate; this is the rationale for patent protection.

column1: Potential benefit of monopoly: how can innovation help a monopolist keep its abnormal profits?
column2: Developing new products that potential rivals cannot produce creates a barrier to entry, deterring rivals from entering the industry.

column1: Why are private, unregulated monopolies illegal in most countries?
column2: Because of their extensive market power, they are held to be undesirable from society's point of view.

column1: Which features of monopolistic competition resemble perfect competition, and which resemble monopoly?
column2:
Like perfect competition: many firms and free entry.
Like monopoly: product differentiation makes each firm a 'mini-monopoly' in its own version of the good (e.g. Adidas, Nike and Puma shoes), so it faces a downward-sloping demand curve.

column1: How can firms differentiate their products through physical and quality differences?
column2:
Physical: size, shape, materials, texture, taste, packaging (e.g. clothes, shoes, processed foods, furniture).
Quality: offering products of different quality.

column1: How can firms differentiate their products through location?
column2: By locating where customers have easy access, e.g. hotels near airports and convenience stores in residential areas.

column1: How can firms differentiate their products through services?
column2: By offering home delivery, product demonstrations, free support, warranties and attractive purchase terms.

column1: How can firms differentiate their products through product image?
column2: By celebrity advertising or endorsements, brand names and attractive packaging.

column1: Compare the demand curves facing a firm in perfect competition, monopolistic competition and monopoly.
column2:
Perfect competition: perfectly elastic (horizontal).
Monopolistic competition: downward-sloping and relatively elastic (flatter).
Monopoly: downward-sloping and less elastic (steeper).

column1: If a firm raises its price, how do its lost sales compare in perfect competition, monopoly and monopolistic competition?
column2:
Perfect competition: it loses all sales.
Monopoly: it loses only some, as there is no alternative product.
Monopolistic competition: it loses more than a monopolist (substitutes exist) but fewer than a perfectly competitive firm (substitutes are not perfect).

column1: Why does a firm in monopolistic competition have less market power than a monopolist?
column2: Its product has many close (though imperfect) substitutes that consumers can switch to, so its demand curve is more elastic.

column1: Distinguish between price competition and non-price competition.
column2:
Price competition: lowering the price to attract customers away from rivals.
Non-price competition: attracting customers by other means, mainly product differentiation, advertising and branding.

column1: How do successful product differentiation, advertising and branding affect a monopolistically competitive firm?
column2: Consumers are convinced the product is superior → demand shifts right and becomes steeper (less elastic) → more market power, so the firm can raise its price without losing many buyers → larger potential short-run profits.

column1: Which monopolistically competitive firms have to rely more on price competition?
column2: Firms less able to build consumer loyalty, whose products are less differentiated from substitutes.

column1: How does the short-run equilibrium of a firm in monopolistic competition compare with that of a monopolist?
column2: The analysis is identical (output where MR = MC; compare the price on the demand curve with AC), except that the demand curve is flatter (more elastic). The firm can make abnormal profit, normal profit or a loss.

column1: Firms in monopolistic competition earn abnormal profits in the short run. Explain the long-run adjustment.
column2: Abnormal profits → new firms enter and attract customers away → demand facing each existing firm falls (shifts left) → until demand is just tangent to AC → price equals AC: normal profit.

column1: Firms in monopolistic competition make losses in the short run. Explain the long-run adjustment.
column2: Losses → some firms leave the industry → their customers switch to the remaining firms → each remaining firm's demand rises (shifts right) → until losses disappear and price equals AC: normal profit.

column1: Describe the long-run equilibrium diagram of a firm in monopolistic competition.
column2: The downward-sloping demand curve is tangent to (just touches) the AC curve at the output where MR = MC, so price equals AC (normal profit), while price is above MC.

column1: How does long-run adjustment to normal profit differ between perfect competition and monopolistic competition?
column2:
Perfect competition: entry and exit shift industry supply and change the market price each firm takes.
Monopolistic competition: entry and exit shift each firm's own downward-sloping demand curve until it is tangent to AC.

column1: Why does monopolistic competition fail to achieve allocative efficiency?
column2: In long-run equilibrium, price is above MC at the profit-maximising output, so resources are underallocated to the good (society would like more of it): market failure.

column1: What is meant by saying that some inefficiency is the 'price' of product variety in monopolistic competition?
column2: Consumers gain product variety but give up some allocative efficiency, whereas perfect competition achieves efficiency at the cost of zero product variety.

column1: Why do some economists argue that monopolistic competition produces too much product variety?
column2: Too many brands (e.g. of breakfast cereals, detergents or cars) confuse consumers, and the high costs of advertising and new product development lead to higher prices; consumers might be better off with less variety and lower prices.

column1: What do monopolistic competition and perfect competition have in common?
column2: A large number of firms; free entry (no barriers); and abnormal profit or loss in the short run but only normal profit in the long run.

column1: Compare monopolistic competition and perfect competition in terms of market power and allocative efficiency.
column2:
Perfect competition: no market power (horizontal demand curve) and allocatively efficient in the long run.
Monopolistic competition: some market power (downward-sloping demand), price above MC, so consumers pay more: market failure.

column1: Compare monopolistic competition and perfect competition in terms of product variety and economies of scale.
column2:
Variety: none in perfect competition (identical products); plenty in monopolistic competition, usually an advantage to consumers.
Economies of scale: none in perfect competition (tiny firms); only small ones in monopolistic competition (firms relatively small).

column1: What do monopolistic competition and monopoly have in common?
column2: Both face downward-sloping demand curves with MR below demand, so at the profit-maximising output price exceeds MC: neither is allocatively efficient (market failure).

column1: Compare monopolistic competition and monopoly in terms of the number and size of firms, barriers to entry and long-run profit.
column2:
Monopolistic competition: many small firms, free entry, normal profit in the long run.
Monopoly: one (or one dominant) very large firm, high barriers to entry, abnormal profit possible in the long run.

column1: Why are prices likely to be lower, and output higher, in monopolistic competition than in monopoly?
column2: Free entry and exit drive abnormal profits to zero in the long run, and the availability of substitutes reduces each firm's market power; a monopoly's barriers to entry let it keep abnormal profits and a higher price.

column1: Compare monopolistic competition and monopoly in terms of pressure on costs.
column2: Competition among firms in monopolistic competition puts downward pressure on costs and may force less efficient firms out; a monopoly faces no such pressure.

column1: Compare monopolistic competition and monopoly in terms of research and development.
column2: Monopolies' long-run abnormal profits make it easier to finance R&D, but competitive pressure may push monopolistically competitive firms to pursue R&D for product development to keep or increase their sales.

column1: Compare monopolistic competition and monopoly in terms of economies of scale and product variety.
column2:
Economies of scale: much greater potential in monopoly (even natural monopoly), which can lower prices; only small ones in monopolistic competition.
Variety: far greater in monopolistic competition, with many firms producing substitutes.

column1: What does 'oligopoly' mean literally, and what kind of industry does it describe?
column2: From the Greek for 'few sellers': an industry dominated by a small number of large firms, which may vary in size.

column1: What barriers to entry protect oligopolies? Give examples.
column2: All the barriers found in monopoly: economies of scale (aircraft, cars), legal barriers such as patents (pharmaceuticals), control of natural resources (oil, copper, silver), aggressive tactics; plus the high start-up costs of developing a new or differentiated product.

column1: Why are high start-up costs a particular barrier to entry in oligopoly?
column2: Established oligopolies spend enormous sums on product differentiation and advertising, which new firms find very difficult to match.

column1: How does decision-making by oligopolistic firms differ from that of firms in perfect and monopolistic competition?
column2: Firms in perfect and monopolistic competition are so numerous that they act independently, ignoring rivals' possible actions. Oligopolists are few and mutually interdependent: one firm's decisions shift the demand curves facing the others, so they watch their rivals closely.

column1: What is strategic behaviour in oligopoly?
column2: Planning actions that take rivals' possible courses of action into account, like playing chess or cards: firms try hard to guess rivals' actions and reactions before forming their own strategy.

column1: What is collusion?
column2: An agreement between firms to limit competition between them, usually by fixing price (and so lowering the quantity produced).

column1: What is the incentive to collude in oligopoly?
column2: Collusion reduces the uncertainty of not knowing how rivals will behave, and maximises profits for the industry as a whole.

column1: What is the incentive to compete, or to cheat, in oligopoly?
column2: Each firm hopes to capture part of its rivals' market shares and profits; within a collusive agreement, each can raise its profit at its partners' expense by secretly cutting its price.

column1: What is a price war?
column2: When one firm's price cut is matched by retaliatory price cuts from rivals, leaving all firms collectively worse off with lower prices and profits, possibly even with prices below average cost (losses).

column1: Why do oligopolistic firms go to great lengths to avoid price competition?
column2: Rivals are likely to match any price cut, triggering a price war that leaves all firms with lower prices and profits; so they prefer non-price competition.

column1: What is game theory, and whose work is it based on?
column2: A mathematical technique for analysing the behaviour of interdependent decision-makers who act strategically. It is based heavily on the work of John F. Nash, who shared the 1994 Nobel Prize in Economics with John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten.

column1: What is a payoff matrix?
column2: A table showing each possible combination of the players' strategies (e.g. high or low price for each of two firms) and the payoff (profit) each player receives in each combination.

column1: What is the prisoner's dilemma?
column2: A situation where two rational decision-makers, each acting strategically to maximise their own payoff by trying to outguess the other, end up collectively worse off: a conflict between individual self-interest and the collective interest.

column1: What is the Nash equilibrium in the oligopoly pricing game?
column2: The final position of the game: both firms choose the low-price strategy and earn low profits, even though both would be better off cooperating at a high price.

column1: Two oligopolists have agreed to charge a high price. According to the payoff matrix, why is each tempted to cheat?
column2: If one secretly cuts its price while the other keeps the high price, the cheat captures a large share of the rival's sales and earns much higher profit, while the rival's profit falls to very little.

column1: Using the prisoner's dilemma, explain why two oligopolists who agree on a high price tend to end up both charging low prices.
column2: Each fears the other will cheat (leaving it with the lowest profit) and wants the cheat's high profit → each cuts its price to beat the other → both end up with low prices and low profits: the Nash equilibrium.

column1: Which real-world features of oligopoly does the prisoner's dilemma game illustrate?
column2: Interdependence, strategic behaviour, conflicting incentives (collude versus cheat), the way price competition (price wars) leaves all firms worse off, and hence firms' strong interest in non-price competition.

column1: How does the role of price competition differ between monopolistic competition and oligopoly?
column2: Monopolistically competitive firms compete on both price and non-price factors. Oligopolists go to great lengths to avoid price competition but engage in intense non-price competition.

column1: What forms does non-price competition take in oligopoly?
column2: Product development, advertising, branding, and services such as quality customer service, warranties, provision of credit and discounts on upgrades.

column1: Why can oligopolists engage in more non-price competition than monopolistically competitive firms?
column2: Their large profits give them considerable financial resources to devote to R&D, advertising and branding.

column1: How does developing new products benefit an oligopolistic firm?
column2: New products give a competitive edge → greater market power and less elastic demand for the firm's product → opportunities for substantially higher sales and profits.

column1: Why is product differentiation a safer way for an oligopolist to raise profits than cutting its price?
column2: It does not invite immediate retaliation: rivals need time and resources to develop competing products, whereas a price cut can be matched at once.

column1: What is collusive oligopoly, and what is the most common form of collusion?
column2: Firms agree among themselves to limit competition, increase market power and raise profits. The most common form is price fixing (holding prices constant, raising them by a fixed amount, or fixing price differences between products).

column1: Why is collusion illegal in most countries?
column2: It limits competition: like an unregulated monopoly, it raises prices, reduces output and is held to be against consumers' and society's interests.

column1: What is a cartel?
column2: A formal agreement between firms in an industry to limit competition in order to increase profits, e.g. by fixing each firm's output (raising the price), fixing the price, dividing up the market, or setting up barriers to entry.

column1: Diagram: how does a price-fixing cartel maximise profit?
column2: Exactly like a monopoly: using industry demand and MR and the sum of the members' MC curves, the cartel produces where MR = MC and sets the price from the demand curve. Total output is then divided among the members.

column1: How can cartel members divide up the profit-maximising output?
column2: By agreeing market shares based on their historical shares, or by competing for shares through non-price competition (product differentiation and advertising).

column1: What is the best-known cartel, and how does it raise prices?
column2: OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries): each member country is assigned an output quota, and restricting total oil output raises the world price.

column1: What do firms gain from forming a cartel?
column2: Increased market power (control over price), higher profits from higher prices, and no more competition or uncertainty about what rivals will do.

column1: Why is it difficult for authorities to act against cartels?
column2: It is hard to discover and prove that a cartel exists, so there may be far more collusion than is ever detected.

column1: Why does the incentive to cheat threaten cartels?
column2: Each member can gain by secretly lowering its price for some buyers; if many members cheat, or cheating is discovered, the cartel may collapse.

column1: How do cost differences between firms and the number of firms make cartels hard to maintain?
column2: With a common price, high-cost members make lower profits than low-cost members, making agreement difficult; and the more firms there are, the harder it is to agree on price and on each firm's output.

column1: How can cheating within a cartel lead to a price war?
column2: One member's price cut → retaliatory price cuts by the others → prices and profits fall for all members, leaving the industry collectively worse off.

column1: What is informal collusion?
column2: Implicit, understood cooperation between firms without a formal agreement, aiming to coordinate prices, avoid price-cutting, limit competition, reduce uncertainty and raise profits.

column1: What is price leadership? Give examples.
column2: Informal collusion in which a dominant firm (the largest or lowest-cost) sets the price and initiates any changes; the others follow as price-takers but compete on non-price factors. Price changes are infrequent. Examples: airlines, supermarkets, fast food restaurants.

column1: What is non-collusive oligopoly?
column2: Oligopolistic firms that do not collude in any way to fix or coordinate prices: each behaves independently, but still strategically, taking rivals' possible reactions into account.

column1: What price behaviour is commonly observed in real-world oligopolies?
column2: Prices tend to be rigid (stable over long periods), and when they do change, they tend to change together for all firms in the industry.

column1: Why might a non-colluding oligopolist decide not to raise its price?
column2: It expects rivals not to follow → rivals keep their lower prices and take some of its customers → its sales and profits fall.

column1: Why might a non-colluding oligopolist decide not to cut its price?
column2: It expects rivals to match the cut → it gains few customers, ends up with a lower price and possibly lower profits, and risks setting off a price war.

column1: What does the strategic reasoning of non-colluding oligopolists explain?
column2: Why prices are stable even without collusion, why firms do not compete on price, and why each firm must consider rivals' reactions to avoid lower revenues, lower profits and price instability.

column1: What is a concentration ratio?
column2: A measure of market concentration: the percentage of an industry's total output produced by its largest firms (e.g. the 4-firm concentration ratio).

column1: What does it mean if the 4-firm concentration ratio of an industry is 45%?
column2: The four largest firms in the industry produce 45% of the industry's total output.

column1: Why is it useful to know an industry's concentration ratio?
column2: It shows how concentrated output is among the largest firms, giving clues as to whether oligopolies have too much market power.

column1: What do high and low concentration ratios indicate?
column2:
High: a low degree of competition.
Low: a greater degree of competition.

column1: At what concentration ratio is an industry generally considered oligopolistic?
column2: When the four largest firms control 40% of output (an arbitrary cut-off point).

column1: In US manufacturing, which industries had the highest and lowest concentration ratios among those compared?
column2: Transportation equipment was the most concentrated (4-firm ratio about 64%) and furniture the least (about 19%).

column1: Why may a national concentration ratio misjudge competition because of international trade?
column2: It ignores competition from imports, and it gives no indication of firms' importance in the global market, where they may be dominant even if there is domestic competition.

column1: Why do concentration ratios ignore competition from other industries?
column2: They do not account for substitutes produced by other industries, e.g. aluminium competes with copper, so the aluminium industry's concentration would be lower if measured together with copper.

column1: Why can two industries with the same concentration ratio have very different degrees of market power?
column2: Concentration ratios do not show the relative sizes of the largest firms: a 3-firm ratio of 90% could be three firms with 30% each, or one with 60% and two with 15%.

column1: Why do both collusive and non-collusive oligopolies cause market failure?
column2: Collusive oligopolies behave like a monopoly; non-collusive firms also face downward-sloping demand curves and produce below the output that maximises social surplus. Both cause welfare loss and allocative inefficiency.

column1: Criticisms of oligopoly: what market outcomes does it share with monopoly?
column2: Welfare loss and market failure; higher prices and lower output than under competitive conditions; loss of consumer surplus to the oligopolists, since price exceeds MC.

column1: Criticisms of oligopoly: besides price and output, what other problems does it share with monopoly?
column2: Negative impacts on income distribution, possibly higher production costs because of the lack of price competition, and possibly less innovation.

column1: What criticism applies to oligopoly beyond those it shares with monopoly?
column2: Many countries have anti-monopoly laws, but collusion is difficult to detect and prove, so oligopolists may collude, behave like monopolies and get away with it.

column1: What benefits does oligopoly share with monopoly?
column2: Economies of scale from large size (lower costs and prices); abnormal profits that can fund product development and innovation; and cost-reducing innovations that may be passed on as lower prices.

column1: Why is innovation a more important benefit in oligopoly than in monopoly?
column2: Non-price competition forces oligopolists to innovate in order to increase their market share and profits.

column1: What advantage does oligopoly offer consumers compared with monopoly in terms of choice?
column2: Product development increases product variety, giving consumers greater choice, whereas a monopoly offers little differentiation and variety.

column1: In 2019, what did 44 US states allege against 20 pharmaceutical companies?
column2: Illegal collusion: conspiracies to fix prices and divide market shares for over 100 generic medicines (including diabetes and cancer treatments), stopping prices from falling or raising them, in some cases by more than 1000%.

column1: What are the potential advantages of large firms with significant market power?
column2: Large economies of scale (including natural monopoly) that lower costs, and abnormal profits that can finance research and development of new products and technologies (innovation).

column1: What risks do markets dominated by large firms pose for prices, output and consumer choice?
column2: Higher prices and lower output than under competition (price above MC, welfare loss), loss of consumer surplus to the large firms, and reduced quality and choice of products.

column1: What is a markup over marginal cost, and why does it indicate market power?
column2: The amount added to marginal cost to obtain the price. The bigger the markup, the more the firm is able to charge a price above marginal cost, which is market power.

column1: What did a 2019 IMF study find about market concentration?
column2: Markups over marginal cost for 900,000 firms in 27 countries rose by 8% on average between 2000 and 2015 (most in the US), driven by a small share of firms, and mergers and acquisitions were followed by significantly higher markups.

column1: According to the 2019 IMF study, what harm results from rising market power?
column2: Less investment in physical capital (lowering GDP growth), workers receiving a smaller share of the value they create (more income inequality), and possibly less innovation as competitive pressure weakens.

column1: What is abuse of market power (anti-competitive practices)?
column2: Firms engaging in activities that reduce competition. According to the European Commission, a dominant position is not anti-competitive in itself, but exploiting it to eliminate competition is an abuse.

column1: Give examples of abuse of a dominant market position, as identified by the European Commission.
column2: Charging unreasonably high prices; selling at artificially low prices that smaller rivals cannot match; forcing buyers to take a product artificially tied to a popular one; refusing to deal with some customers or giving discounts for buying all supplies from the dominant firm; making one sale conditional on another.

column1: Why are monopolies and collusive oligopolies the main targets of government action against abuse of market power?
column2: Monopolies have the most market power, which is abusive because there is no competition (private unregulated monopolies are illegal almost everywhere); collusive oligopolies have monopoly-like power, so collusion is illegal almost everywhere.

column1: Do non-collusive oligopolies and firms in monopolistic competition abuse their market power?
column2: Non-collusive oligopolies may or may not, depending on the situation. Firms in monopolistic competition mostly do not, because there is significant competition from firms producing substitutes.

column1: What is competition policy?
column2: Laws that promote competition by preventing collusion between oligopolistic firms and anti-competitive behaviour by a single dominant firm. Offending firms are usually fined, or may be broken up into smaller firms.

column1: Why is competition law difficult to interpret and apply?
column2: People differ on what counts as anti-competitive behaviour and the laws may be vague; the OECD calls deciding when behaviour is abuse rather than competitive action one of the most complex and controversial areas of competition policy.

column1: Why is competition law enforced more strictly by some governments than others?
column2: It depends on their priorities and political or ideological views: some believe strict enforcement is needed to protect consumers and achieve allocative efficiency; others believe competitive market forces achieve this on their own over time. It is a normative question.

column1: Why is collusion difficult to prosecute under competition law?
column2: Because it is illegal, collusion happens in secret, so evidence is hard to find and prove.

column1: What is a merger, and why do firms merge?
column2: An agreement between two or more firms to join together into a single firm, to capture economies of scale (lower average costs), to grow, or to acquire market power.

column1: Why are mergers an issue for competition policy, and how are they usually controlled?
column2: The single firm created may have too much market power, so legislation usually limits the size of the combined firm.

column1: What are the difficulties with merger policies?
column2: Uncertainty about which firms should be allowed to merge, arising from problems of interpreting the legislation and from ideological differences between governments about how much market power is acceptable.

column1: Why did the UK's Competition and Markets Authority block the 2019 merger of Asda and Sainsbury's?
column2: The combined firm would have had a 30.7% market share, becoming the UK's largest supermarket. The firms claimed cost savings would cut prices by up to 10%, but the CMA found the merger would raise prices and reduce quality and choice for shoppers.

column1: Why did the European Commission fine Google $5 billion in 2018?
column2: For requiring phone manufacturers to preinstall Google Search and the Chrome browser to get access to the Google Play app store, which denied rivals the chance to innovate and compete and denied consumers effective competition.

column1: What are the arguments for and against breaking up big tech companies?
column2:
For (Senator Elizabeth Warren): they have too much power over the economy, society and democracy, crush competition, profit from private data, hurt small businesses and stifle innovation.
Against (economist Tyler Cowen): they are major innovators, and breaking them up could weaken innovation.

column1: What is the main weakness of fines as a response to abuse of market power?
column2: Firms calculate whether breaking the law is more profitable than complying; the profits from abusing market power are often large enough to make paying the fines worthwhile.

column1: Why are firms that abuse their market power often not caught and fined?
column2: Because of the political climate, or because firms are careful to cover up their actions.

column1: Give examples of fines imposed on banks for rigging foreign exchange markets.
column2: In 2019 the EU fined Barclays, J.P. Morgan, MUFG and Royal Bank of Scotland $1.2 billion for rigging the forex market for 11 currencies, and US regulators fined a group of banks $2.8 billion for rigging exchange rates.

column1: Why was the Swiss bank UBS exempted from the EU's 2019 forex-rigging fine?
column2: It alerted the European Union to the existence of the two cartels.

column1: Give examples of EU fines on technology firms for abuse of market power.
column2: Google: €2.7 billion (2017, favouring Google Shopping in search results) and €5 billion (2018, Android preinstallation). Qualcomm: $1.2 billion (2018, payments to Apple to use its chips). Intel: $1.45 billion (2009, discounts for not using rival AMD's chips).

column1: What is nationalisation, and how can it address the problems of natural monopoly?
column2: The transfer of ownership from the private sector to the government. Owning the natural monopoly lets the government make it lower prices and raise output in consumers' interests, reducing allocative inefficiency and welfare loss.

column1: What is the drawback of government ownership of natural monopolies, and what trend has followed?
column2: Government firms are not driven to maximise profits, so they may be inefficient with higher than necessary costs. Since the 1990s there has been a worldwide trend to privatise government enterprises.

column1: What is privatisation?
column2: The opposite of nationalisation: transferring ownership of an enterprise from the government to the private sector.

column1: Can a natural monopoly be regulated while it stays privately owned?
column2: Yes: governments can regulate its price (marginal cost pricing or average cost pricing) to achieve more socially desirable price and quantity outcomes.

column1: What is marginal cost pricing for a regulated natural monopoly?
column2: The government forces the monopoly to charge a price equal to marginal cost (P = MC), achieving allocative efficiency with a lower price and a higher quantity.

column1: Why is marginal cost pricing an unpopular way to regulate a natural monopoly?
column2: Average cost is still falling, so MC is below AC → a price equal to MC is below AC → the firm makes losses → it goes out of business unless the government subsidises it.

column1: What is average cost pricing for a regulated natural monopoly?
column2: The government forces the firm to charge a price equal to average cost (P = AC), so it earns normal profit. Price is higher and quantity lower than under marginal cost pricing, but price is lower and quantity higher than for an unregulated monopolist.

column1: What are the advantages of average cost pricing for a natural monopoly?
column2: The monopolist earns normal profit, so it is in no danger of shutting down, and the outcome is more efficient than the unregulated market outcome (though not allocatively efficient).

column1: Why does average cost pricing weaken a natural monopoly's incentive to keep costs low?
column2: It is guaranteed a price equal to its average costs, so if costs rise through inefficiency it still receives a price covering them, unlike an unregulated profit-maximiser.

column1: How can continued regulation of a natural monopoly protect it from competition it should face?
column2: If technological change (e.g. in telecommunications) means it is no longer a natural monopoly, continued regulation may shield it from new competitors that could produce more efficiently.
